metaDescription: Estimate take-home pay per paycheck after 2026 federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare. Compare filing statuses and pre-tax retirement contributions.
introText:
At $60,000, a single filer keeps an estimated $50,390 a year before state tax. That is $1,938.08 per biweekly paycheck after federal income tax and payroll tax. The paycheck calculator above starts with annual gross pay and biweekly checks, but you can enter pay per paycheck and choose a different schedule.

It shows take-home pay per check as the headline result, with each deduction shown per check and per year. The result estimates annual federal tax liability for a W-2 employee who takes the standard deduction. It does not predict the exact amount an employer will withhold.

For the worked example, enter $60,000 in annual gross pay, choose single filing and leave pre-tax retirement at $0. The standard deduction leaves $43,900 of taxable income. Federal income tax comes to $5,020, while Social Security takes $3,720 and Medicare takes $870.

Together, those payroll taxes are $4,590. Subtract federal and payroll tax from gross pay to get $50,390 for the year. Across 26 biweekly checks, that is $1,938.08 per check, or 84.0% of gross pay.

State tax, credits and other withholding could change what appears on a pay stub.
howItWorks:
The paycheck calculator estimates annual take-home pay, then divides it by the number of checks in your pay schedule. Annual take-home pay equals gross pay minus pre-tax retirement contributions, federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare. For the $60,000 single-filer example, the result is $50,390 a year and $1,938.08 across 26 biweekly checks. You can enter gross pay by year or by paycheck. The schedule choices are weekly, every two weeks, twice a month and monthly, with 52, 26, 24 and 12 checks respectively. If you need to convert a pay figure before entering it, use the [salary calculator](/salary-calculator/).

Federal income tax starts with taxable income: gross pay minus your annual pre-tax retirement contribution and the standard deduction, with a floor of zero. The calculator applies the [Internal Revenue Service (IRS) 2026 brackets](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/rp-25-32.pdf) band by band to that amount. For a single filer earning $60,000, taxable income is $43,900. The first $12,400 is taxed at 10%, producing $1,240. The remaining $31,500 is taxed at 12%, producing $3,780. Those bands add up to $5,020 in federal income tax. Being in a higher bracket does not apply that bracket's rate to every dollar of taxable income.

Social Security is 6.2% of gross wages up to the $184,500 wage base. Medicare is 1.45% of all gross wages, with an additional 0.9% withheld on wages above $200,000. These payroll taxes use gross wages even when a pre-tax retirement contribution lowers taxable income. For example, Social Security on a $300,000 salary stops at $11,439, while Medicare comes to $5,250. On a $250,000 salary, Medicare is $4,075, including $450 in Additional Medicare withholding. The calculator shows Social Security and Medicare separately.

A pre-tax retirement contribution lowers the income used to calculate federal income tax, but it does not lower the gross wages used for Social Security or Medicare. On a $100,000 single-filer salary, a $10,000 contribution reduces federal income tax from $13,170 to $10,970. Social Security stays at $6,200, and Medicare stays at $1,450. Annual take-home pay is $71,380 with the contribution, compared with $79,180 without it. The contribution lowers take-home pay by $7,800 because federal income tax falls by $2,200. Enter the contribution as an annual amount, even if you enter gross pay per paycheck.

sections.heading: 2026 Federal Figures Used
sections.body:
The paycheck calculator uses the following 2026 standard deductions, income tax brackets and payroll tax figures.

| Item | 2026 figure | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Standard deduction, single | $16,100 | [IRS 2026 adjustments](https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/irs-releases-tax-inflation-adjustments-for-tax-year-2026-including-amendments-from-the-one-big-beautiful-bill) |
| Standard deduction, married filing jointly | $32,200 | [IRS 2026 adjustments](https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/irs-releases-tax-inflation-adjustments-for-tax-year-2026-including-amendments-from-the-one-big-beautiful-bill) |
| Standard deduction, head of household | $24,150 | [IRS 2026 adjustments](https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/irs-releases-tax-inflation-adjustments-for-tax-year-2026-including-amendments-from-the-one-big-beautiful-bill) |
| Income tax rates | 10%, 12%, 22%, 24%, 32%, 35%, 37% | [IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-32](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/rp-25-32.pdf) |
| Single, top of the 10% and 12% brackets | $12,400 and $50,400 of taxable income | [IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-32](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/rp-25-32.pdf) |
| Social Security tax | 6.2% up to $184,500 of wages | [IRS Topic 751](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc751) |
| Medicare tax | 1.45% of all wages | [IRS Topic 751](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc751) |
| Additional Medicare withholding | 0.9% of wages above $200,000 | [IRS Topic 751](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc751) |

For more detail on where taxable income falls, use the [federal tax bracket calculator](/tax-bracket-calculator/). The figures above were checked on the linked IRS pages on 2026-11-15.

sections.heading: Take-Home Pay at Different Salaries
sections.body:
In our internal modeling, we ran 2026 federal brackets and payroll tax across salaries from $40,000 to $150,000 to estimate take-home pay. The table assumes a single filer taking the standard deduction, with no state tax, retirement contribution or other deductions. Each biweekly figure spreads the annual estimate across 26 checks. These figures are modeled results, so your entries in the paycheck calculator above may produce different amounts.

| Gross salary | Federal income tax | Social Security | Medicare | Take-home per year | Take-home per biweekly check | Share of gross |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $40,000 | $2,620 | $2,480 | $580 | $34,320 | $1,320.00 | 85.8% |
| $60,000 | $5,020 | $3,720 | $870 | $50,390 | $1,938.08 | 84.0% |
| $100,000 | $13,170 | $6,200 | $1,450 | $79,180 | $3,045.38 | 79.2% |
| $150,000 | $24,734 | $9,300 | $2,175 | $113,791 | $4,376.58 | 75.9% |

The take-home share falls from 85.8% to 75.9% across the table as more taxable income reaches higher brackets. Social Security stops applying once wages reach $184,500. Pre-tax retirement can change the income-tax part of the result: a $10,000 contribution lowers take-home pay by $7,800 in the $100,000 single-filer case. Filing status changes the estimate too. At $60,000, married filing jointly produces $52,570 in annual take-home pay, or $2,021.92 per biweekly check. Head of household at $60,000 produces $51,462 annually and $1,979.31 per biweekly check. Choose the filing status that applies to the estimate you want to see. Married filing separately is not offered.

sections.heading: What This Estimate Leaves Out
sections.body:
The paycheck calculator leaves out taxes, deductions and withholding choices that can change the amount on an actual pay stub.

- State and local income tax.
- Tax credits, including the child tax credit.
- Itemized deductions.
- Health premiums, health savings account (HSA) contributions and other pre-tax items.
- Extra withholding requested on Form W-4.
- Tips, overtime, senior and qualified business income (QBI) deductions.

This is an annual-liability estimate using the standard deduction. It does not calculate withholding under IRS Publication 15-T. An employer's actual check can therefore differ from the calculator's per-check figure. The calculator models 0.9% Additional Medicare withholding above $200,000 for every filing status. Final Additional Medicare liability uses different thresholds, including $250,000 for married filing jointly, as explained in [IRS Topic 560](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc560). A married couple's final liability can therefore differ from the Additional Medicare amount withheld.

This paycheck calculator is not suited to self-employed or 1099 income, multiple jobs or itemized deductions. Use figures that account for those circumstances instead. State tax, credits or extra W-4 withholding would also change the answer, so treat the result as an estimate rather than personalized withholding advice. Enter your gross pay and filing status in the paycheck calculator above, then compare its result with your pay stub.

faqs.question: How much of my paycheck will I keep after taxes?
faqs.answer: At $60,000 a year, a single filer keeps an estimated $50,390 before state tax. That is $1,938.08 per biweekly check, or 84.0% of gross pay. The estimate subtracts federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare. Enter your own pay in the calculator above because filing status and pre-tax retirement contributions can change the result.

faqs.question: Is a paycheck calculator accurate?
faqs.answer: It is an estimate of annual federal tax liability and take-home pay under the listed assumptions. It uses the standard deduction and does not calculate an employer's exact withholding under IRS Publication 15-T. State tax, credits and health premiums are also left out. Compare the per-check result with a pay stub if you need to understand a difference.

faqs.question: How do I calculate my paycheck manually?
faqs.answer: Start with annual gross pay and subtract pre-tax retirement contributions and the standard deduction to find taxable income. Apply the federal brackets to taxable income band by band. Then subtract federal income tax, Social Security, Medicare and the retirement contribution from gross pay. Divide annual take-home pay by the number of checks in your chosen pay schedule.

faqs.question: Does this paycheck calculator include state tax?
faqs.answer: No. The paycheck calculator does not subtract state or local income tax. Its take-home figure is therefore before those taxes. If state or local tax appears on your pay stub, that is one reason the actual net check can be lower than this estimate.

faqs.question: Why is my real paycheck different from this estimate?
faqs.answer: Your employer's withholding can differ from this annual-liability estimate. The calculator also leaves out state tax, credits, health premiums and extra W-4 withholding. It does not model tips or overtime deductions. Compare the deduction rows with your pay stub to identify which amounts the estimate leaves out.

faqs.question: How does a 401(k) contribution change my take-home pay?
faqs.answer: A pre-tax retirement contribution reduces the income used for federal income tax, while Social Security and Medicare still use gross wages. In the $100,000 single-filer case, a $10,000 contribution lowers federal income tax by $2,200. Take-home pay falls by $7,800 rather than the full contribution amount. Enter your annual contribution to see the change in the calculator.

faqs.question: Why does Social Security tax stop on high salaries?
faqs.answer: Social Security tax applies only up to the 2026 wage base of $184,500. The employee rate is 6.2%, so the modeled Social Security tax on a $300,000 salary is $11,439. Medicare still applies to gross wages above the Social Security wage base. The calculator shows both taxes separately in its results.

faqs.question: Does a paycheck calculator include Medicare tax?
faqs.answer: Yes. This paycheck calculator subtracts Medicare tax at 1.45% of gross wages. It also models an extra 0.9% withheld on wages above $200,000. Final Additional Medicare liability can use a different threshold for married filing jointly, so that withholding estimate may differ from the final tax.
